204.title: The body is the field (13.1–13.6)
204.hook: the Gita began on a battlefield; chapter thirteen says the real field is you
204.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often use Gita 13's field and knower of the field (kshetra and kshetrajna) in meditation and study, as a way of noticing the body and mind as something known, and asking who the knower is.

segments.voice: Yesterday, priya: the one dear to me, a portrait of the devoted person. Your line was free from hate, friendly to all. Today, a new chapter, and a new picture.

Go back to the Gita's very first line. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks: on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? Dharmakshetre, kurukshetre. The whole book opens on a field. Two armies, dust, chariots, a man about to break down. Twelve chapters later, chapter thirteen picks up that same word, field, kshetra, and turns it around. The field, Krishna says, isn't only out there where the armies stand. You're standing in it. You are it.
screen: `ON THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` → `TWO ARMIES, ONE FIELD.` → `THE FIELD IS YOU.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen opens with a definition. This body, Arjuna, is called the field, and the one who knows it, the sages call the knower of the field. Kshetra, the field. Kshetrajna, the knower of the field. Picture a farmer's field. Weeds and wheat grow there. Weather passes over it. Seasons change it. And at the edge stands someone who watches it and knows it, who isn't the dirt. Then the line that makes this chapter famous: know me also as the knower of the field in all fields. The same knower, in every body. Hindu schools read that line differently. Advaita teachers say the knower in you and the divine knower are finally one. Ramanuja and the Vaishnava schools say the divine dwells in every knower as its inner guide, close but not identical. Both read it from the same verse. Then verses five and six list what's in the field, and the list is bigger than you'd guess. The elements. The sense of I. The intellect. The senses and the mind, and what they reach for. Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the body as a whole, awareness, steadiness. Your wanting, your not wanting, even your moods: all field, things that grow and change and pass. So when anger comes up, the Gita's picture says: something is growing in the field. You can notice it from the edge. You are not only the weather.
screen: `THIS BODY IS CALLED THE FIELD.` · `THE KNOWER OF THE FIELD.` · `THE KNOWER IN ALL FIELDS.` · `EVEN DESIRE AND PAIN ARE FIELD.` · then, large: `THE BODY IS THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Walk the edge of your own field: the body's weight, its warmth, the places that ache; the breath coming and going; a thought arriving, maybe a worry, maybe a wish. Field, all of it. Then, for a moment, notice the one noticing, without naming it, and just watch things grow and pass from the edge.
Kshetra, the field. Gita thirteen: the body, with its senses, desires and moods, is the field; the one who knows it is the knower of the field, kshetrajna.
Your line: the field. The same word the Gita opens with. More of the field tomorrow.

the soul that watches from the edge
the world outside, beyond the body

205.title: Knowledge and its opposite (13.7–13.18)
205.hook: the Gita's list of what knowledge is starts with something you can't look up
205.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote Gita 13.7–13.11 as a checklist of character for students, starting with amanitva, humility; many traditions treat serving and honoring the teacher as part of this knowledge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kshetra: the body is the field, with a knower at its edge. Your line was the field. Today, what the knower actually knows.

The smartest person at a dinner table might have three degrees and win every argument. The wisest person at that table is often someone else, maybe with no degree at all. They just listen longer, and they don't need to be right. The Gita has noticed this too. In chapter thirteen Krishna gives a list with the heading knowledge. You'd expect facts, or philosophy, or a curriculum. Instead the list opens with something no exam can test.
screen: `THE SMARTEST AT THE TABLE.` → `THE WISEST AT THE TABLE.` → `NOT ALWAYS THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Verse seven. The first word on the list is amanitva: humility, not thinking much of yourself. Then adambhitva, no pretending. Then ahimsa, doing no harm, a word you met in camp one. Then patience, straightforwardness, serving your teacher, cleanliness, steadiness, self-control. The list keeps going. Not being dragged by the senses. Not being ruled by the sense of I. Seeing clearly that birth, age, sickness and death bring pain. Not clinging too tightly to home and family. Staying even when things go well and when they don't. Steady devotion. A taste for quiet places, and less need for the crowd. Then Krishna ends with a surprise. This, he says, is called knowledge, and whatever is its opposite is ajnana, ignorance. So in the Gita, knowledge isn't only what's in your head; it's what shows in how you live. A brilliant, arrogant person, by this definition, is missing the first item. From verse twelve the chapter turns to what is to be known, Brahman, and the description goes strange on purpose. It has hands and feet everywhere, eyes and faces everywhere. It shines through every sense, yet has no senses. It's far away, and it's near. It's inside beings and outside them. It seems divided among beings, yet it's undivided. Verse seventeen calls it the light of lights, beyond darkness. The words stretch to point at something words can't hold. And the door to it, the list says, starts with humility.

segments.voice: Think of a recent moment you needed to be right, a text thread, a meeting, a family dinner, and just see it without judging. Now replay it with the need dropped by one notch: maybe you ask a question instead of making a point, or simply listen. Notice how that softer version feels in the chest; that softness is the first item on the Gita's list.
Amanitva, humility, not thinking much of yourself. Gita thirteen, seven to eighteen: knowledge is a way of living that begins with it, and its opposite is ignorance.
Your line: humility first. First on the list, ahead of patience and steadiness. Day two hundred five, done.

206.title: Seeing the same in all (13.19–13.34)
206.hook: one sun lights the whole world; chapter thirteen says one knower lights every field
206.howItsDone: Many Hindus greet others with namaste, often explained as honoring the divine in the other person; Gita 13.27–13.28, seeing the same Lord in all beings, is one of the verses teachers point to for this.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amanitva: knowledge starts with humility, first on the Gita's list. Today, the chapter's last and biggest picture.

Noon light falls on a whole street: the parked cars, the dog on the corner, the neighbor nobody gets along with, the trash can, the rose bush. All of it, at once, the same light. The sun doesn't choose. It doesn't get dirty from shining on the trash, or prettier from shining on the roses. Chapter thirteen ends with that picture, its answer to the question it has circled all chapter: who is the knower of the field?
screen: `NOON LIGHT ON A WHOLE STREET.` → `THE ROSE AND THE TRASH CAN.` → `THE SAME LIGHT ON BOTH.`

segments.voice: First, two words the Gita uses a lot from here on. Prakriti: nature, everything that moves and changes, the body, the senses, the mind. Purusha: the person, the conscious one who experiences it. Verse twenty: nature is behind all doing; the person is behind the experiencing of pleasure and pain. Then verse twenty-seven, the center of today. The one who sees the supreme Lord standing the same in all beings, not perishing when they perish, truly sees. Verse twenty-eight follows: samam pashyan, seeing the same Lord everywhere, such a person doesn't harm the self by the self. Commentators unpack that line in more than one way. Some readers hear in it: if the same one lives in everyone, hurting another is hurting yourself. Verse twenty-nine: the one who sees that nature does the acting, and that the self is not the doer, sees. Two pictures close the chapter. Verse thirty-two: space is everywhere, and it's so subtle it's never stained by what it holds. So the self in every body is never stained. Verse thirty-three: as the one sun lights this whole world, the knower of the field lights the whole field. One light, many fields. The schools differ again on how literally to take the oneness: Advaita as one self, Vaishnava schools as one Lord dwelling in many selves. Either way, the verse asks for one kind of seeing: look at anyone, and look for the light.

segments.voice: Picture a light at your center, steady and warm, then the same light in the person nearest you, in the next room or the next house. Widen it: someone across town, someone on the other side of the world whose name you'll never know, and, if you're willing, someone you find hard. You don't have to like them; just see the same light.
Sama, the same, even. Gita thirteen, twenty-seven: the one who sees the same Lord standing in all beings, imperishable in the perishing, truly sees.
Your line: the one light. It falls on the rose and the trash can alike. See you tomorrow.

207.title: Sattva, rajas, tamas (14.1–14.9)
207.hook: three threads run through everything in nature, and through every mood you've had
207.howItsDone: The three gunas are part of Hindu vocabulary: some people describe foods, habits, music and moods as sattvic, rajasic or tamasic, and Ayurveda and yoga teachers use the terms too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sama: one sun lights the whole world, one knower lights every field. Today, what the field is woven from.

Six in the morning: heavy, foggy, begging for ten more minutes. Ten o'clock: wired, three tabs open, answering messages on the walk to the next thing. And once in a while, around sunset, a clear, quiet moment when everything seems simple and bright. Same person, three different weathers. Hindu thought has names for them, and says they aren't only in people. They're in food, in music, in the whole of nature. Chapter fourteen lays them out.
screen: `FOGGY AT SIX.` → `WIRED AT TEN.` → `CLEAR AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: Verse five. Sattva, rajas, tamas: these gunas, born of nature, bind the undying one in the body. Guna means a quality, and in ordinary Sanskrit it can also mean a strand or a thread, even the cord of a bowstring. So picture a rope of three strands twisted together. Everything in nature is all three, in different mixes. Sattva is clarity, brightness, balance. Verse six: it's clear, it lights things up, it's free of trouble. But even sattva binds, by attachment to happiness and to knowledge. You can get hooked on feeling good and feeling wise. Rajas is passion, motion, heat. Verse seven: it comes from craving and attachment, and binds by attachment to action. It's the part of you that can't stop doing. Tamas is darkness, heaviness, inertia. Verse eight: born of ignorance, it deludes, and binds through carelessness, laziness and sleep. Verse nine sums up: sattva ties you to happiness, rajas to action, and tamas covers understanding and ties you to heedlessness. So none of the three is simply the good one. Even the bright thread is still a thread. And some teachers stress that this is a description, not a verdict: rest needs a little tamas, and getting out of bed needs a little rajas. The point isn't to hate any strand. It's to see the rope. Our word is the first and clearest of the three: sattva.
screen: `GUNA: A QUALITY, A THREAD.` · `SATTVA: CLEAR AND BRIGHT.` · `RAJAS: PASSION AND MOTION.` · `TAMAS: HEAVY AND DARK.` · then, large: `SATTVA.`

segments.voice: Check your own rope right now: heaviness or a pull toward sleep or blankness is the dark thread; buzzing, a list running, a wish to get up and do something is the moving thread; any clarity, even a moment of simply seeing, is the bright one. Don't pick a favorite. Just notice the mix, the way you'd notice the weather.
Sattva. Clarity, brightness, balance: the first of the three gunas, the strands of nature, with rajas, motion, and tamas, heaviness.
Your line: three threads. Clarity, motion, heaviness, twisted into one rope. That's day two hundred seven.

208.title: How they show up (14.10–14.20)
208.hook: the Gita gives field signs for each of the three threads
208.howItsDone: Some Hindus use the gunas as a practical check on daily life, choosing food, company and routines that support sattva; some teachers use Gita 14.11–14.13 to describe what each guna looks like.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sattva: clarity, motion and heaviness, twisted together like a rope. Today, how to spot each one.

Birdwatchers don't need to see the whole bird. A flash of red on the wing, a certain call at dawn, the way it flies in loops, and they know. They call those field marks. Chapter fourteen does the same for the three gunas. Krishna gives the field marks: what each one looks like when it's winning, in a person, in a room, maybe in you this afternoon. It reads almost like a checklist.
screen: `A FLASH OF RED, A CALL AT DAWN.` → `FIELD MARKS.` → `FOR THE THREE THREADS.`

segments.voice: Verse ten starts with a rule: one thread rises by pushing down the other two. Sattva comes up by overpowering rajas and tamas, rajas by overpowering sattva and tamas, and tamas by overpowering the other two. The mix is always shifting. Then the field marks. Verse eleven: when light and understanding shine through every gate of the body, the eyes, the ears, the mind, sattva is strong. Verse twelve: greed, busyness, starting one project after another, restlessness, longing. That's rajas rising. Verse thirteen: darkness, sluggishness, carelessness, confusion. That's tamas. Then the Gita follows each thread to where it leads. Verse seventeen: from sattva comes knowledge, from rajas greed, from tamas carelessness, confusion and not knowing. Verse eighteen gives a direction: those in sattva rise, those in rajas stay in the middle, those in tamas sink. The chapter even says the thread you're in at the end of life shapes what comes next. Then the turn, verse nineteen. When the seer sees no doer other than the gunas, and knows what is beyond them, that one reaches my being. The threads are moving; the one watching isn't a thread. That's why noticing matters so much. The moment you can say, oh, that's rajas, you're already standing a little outside it.
screen: `ONE RISES, TWO FALL.` · `LIGHT, GREED, OR FOG.` · `KNOWLEDGE, GREED, CONFUSION.` · `THE SEER SEES THE THREADS MOVE.` · then, large: `HOW THEY SHOW UP.`

segments.voice: Scan for field marks: light and clear seeing through the eyes and ears; restlessness, wanting, a pull to start something in the chest and hands; fog, heaviness, a wish to go blank in the head. Whatever is strongest, name it softly: the bright thread, the moving one, or the heavy one. Then rest as the one who noticed.
Rajas, passion, motion, heat. Gita fourteen, ten to twenty: light through every gate is sattva, greed and restlessness are rajas, fog and carelessness are tamas, and the seer watches them move.
Your line: notice yours today. Light, greed or fog: each thread has its field marks. Two hundred eight days now.

209.title: Beyond the three (14.21–14.27)
209.hook: Arjuna asks what a person beyond the three threads looks like
209.carry: the same in praise and blame
209.howItsDone: Hindu teachers hold up the gunatita of Gita 14.22–14.25 as a picture of spiritual maturity; many devotional traditions point to 14.26, unwavering devotion, as the way there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rajas: light through the gates, greed and restlessness, fog, and the seer who watches them move. Today, the one who isn't pulled by any of them.

Post something online and watch what happens to you. A hundred likes, and you feel tall. One cruel comment, and it rattles around your head all night. The hundred don't cancel out the one. Plenty of people are built this way: praise lifts, blame drops, and managing both takes a lot of energy. At the end of chapter fourteen, Arjuna asks a very practical question. What does someone look like who has gone beyond the three threads? How do they act? How do they get there?
screen: `A HUNDRED LIKES.` → `ONE CRUEL COMMENT.` → `WHO ISN'T MOVED BY EITHER?`

segments.voice: Arjuna's question is verse twenty-one, and it has three parts: the marks, the behavior, the way. Krishna answers with a portrait. Verse twenty-two: when light, activity and confusion come, this person doesn't hate them; when they go, doesn't long for them. The threads still show up. Even the person beyond the gunas has sleepy mornings and busy afternoons. The difference is the grip. Verse twenty-three: they sit like someone unconcerned, udasina, literally sitting above, not shaken by the gunas, knowing it's just the threads moving. Verse twenty-four: the same in sorrow and happiness, resting in the self; a lump of clay, a stone and gold are all the same to them. The same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, steady, the same in blame and in praise of themselves. Verse twenty-five: the same in honor and dishonor, the same to friend and enemy. That person, Krishna says, has gone beyond the gunas. Gunatita. Then the answer to the third question, how to get there. Verse twenty-six: the one who serves me with unwavering devotion goes beyond the three and becomes fit for Brahman. So the way beyond isn't a technique for crushing the threads. In this chapter, it's bhakti, love. Verse twenty-seven closes: I am the ground of Brahman, of the deathless, of lasting dharma, and of perfect joy. This isn't indifference. It's the steadiness of someone whose center is somewhere the likes and comments can't reach.
screen: `THE THREADS STILL COME AND GO.` · `SITTING ABOVE, UNSHAKEN.` · `CLAY, STONE AND GOLD, THE SAME.` · `THE WAY BEYOND IS DEVOTION.` · then, large: `BEYOND THE THREE.`

segments.voice: Remember a recent word of praise and let it land; notice the lift in the chest. Then a recent word of blame, and notice the drop. Without pushing either away, sit a little above both, like someone watching weather from a hill: the lift and the drop still come, you're just not living inside them for a moment.
Gunatita, gone beyond the gunas. Gita fourteen: the one who has gone beyond the gunas doesn't hate them when they come or long for them when they go, and is the same in praise and blame.
Your line: the same in praise and blame. The threads still come; they just lose their grip. Until tomorrow.

210.title: The tree with roots above (15.1–15.6)
210.hook: chapter fifteen opens with a sacred fig tree growing upside down
210.howItsDone: The peepal (ashvattha, sacred fig) is honored by Hindus: some water it, tie threads around it and walk around it; Gita 15 uses it as an image of the world, and some recite chapter fifteen on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gunatita: the threads still come and go, but the one beyond them isn't gripped. Now, a tree.

A huge old peepal tree stands at the edge of a village square. Threads are tied around its trunk. Someone walks slow circles around it. Two old men sit in its shade and argue about cricket. Its heart-shaped leaves tremble in the slightest breeze. It's the sacred fig, the ashvattha. Now flip that tree over in your mind: roots up in the sky, branches hanging down, spreading all over the earth. That strange picture is how chapter fifteen begins.

segments.voice: Verse one. They speak of an undying ashvattha tree with its roots above and its branches below. Its leaves are the Vedic hymns. Whoever knows this tree knows the Vedas. The Katha Upanishad describes the same eternal fig with its roots above. So what's the tree? Commentators read it as the whole world of change, samsara, the round of birth and death. Its roots are above because it grows from the highest source. Verse two: its branches spread up and down, fed by the three gunas, and its buds are the objects of the senses. Some roots stretch downward too, into the human world, tangling us in action. That's why the tree feels so real: we're hanging in its branches, and the branches keep growing. Verse three is honest: its real shape can't be seen from here, not its end, not its beginning, not what it stands on. Then the surprise. This huge, deep-rooted tree, Krishna says, cut it down with the strong axe of non-attachment. Asanga, not clinging. Not with violence, not by running away, but by letting go. Verse four: then seek that place from which no one returns, and take refuge in the first person, from whom this ancient flow came. Verse six says that place isn't lit by sun, moon or fire. It's my highest home. This stretch ran through the field, humility, the one light, the three threads, how they show up, and going beyond them. Today it all becomes one picture.

segments.voice: Picture yourself among the branches of a great tree, each branch something you hold on to: a plan, a worry, a person, a wish. Feel your grip on one, and without dropping anything, loosen it a little; that's the axe the Gita means, not clinging. Then let your attention travel up the trunk toward the roots, the source, and rest there.
Ashvattha, the sacred fig. Gita fifteen: the world of change as an upside-down tree, rooted in the highest, cut with the axe of not clinging.
